newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Baseball-More players questioned in Taiwan scandal.
newsitem.headline: Baseball-More players questioned in Taiwan scandal.

text.p: Taiwan investigators on Friday questioned nine more professional baseball players suspected of throwing games in exchange for underworld kickbacks, escalating a scandal that has shaken the island's beloved game.

The latest summonses came one month after the indictment of 13 players of the Chinese Professional Baseball League -- including a former U.S. major league player -- on corruption charges related to alleged game-fixing.

"This is the result of our second round of investigation," Huang Po-lin, the prosecutor who spearheaded the probes, said on state-run television. "We wanted to gather more evidence before bringing in these players."
Prosecutors declined to say if the nine players, all from the China Times Eagles, would be charged. They vowed to press ahead with investigations on more suspected players.
Among the players interrogated were sluggers Liao Min-hsiung and Wang Kuang-hsi, two of the league's most popular stars and heroes of Taiwan's 1992 Olympic silver medal-winning team.
The May charges crowned a year of shocking revelations that stunned followers of baseball, Taiwan's most popular sport.
Among those charged were former Eagle Ravelo Manzanillo, a Dominican star who pitched briefly for the Pittsburgh Pirates, and Taiwan's 1996 most valuable player, Kuo Shang-hao.

Baseball has always been the king of sports on an island whose youth teams long dominated the Little League World Series in the United States and which exulted in the Olympic team's silver medal success at Barcelona.
But the professional league, which began play seven years ago amid much fanfare, says the game-fixing scandal has sent attendances slumping and raised questions over the game's integrity.
The government's charges paint a picture of top players being strong-armed by power mafia figures.
One allegation speaks of four gangsters -- one of them a policeman -- coercing a player at gunpoint to throw games to pay off gambling debts.
Another describes gangsters cornering and roughing up three players after a game whose result did not accord with wagers.
